content: Infant hepatitis B infection significantly increases the likelihood of developing chronic hepatitis B, cirrhosis, or hepatocellular carcinoma (liver cancer) later in life. Perinatal transmission, where the virus is passed from mother to infant during childbirth, is a common mode of infection. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and potential adverse effects of administering the hepatitis B vaccine to pregnant women as a strategy to prevent hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection in their infants. To conduct this review, a search was performed in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register up to August 31, 2014. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared hepatitis B vaccination during pregnancy with either a placebo or no treatment. Quasi-randomized trials and cross-over studies were excluded from consideration. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of trials for inclusion. If any studies had been identified, the plan was to evaluate the risk of bias, extract relevant data, and verify the accuracy of the data. However, no studies meeting the inclusion criteria were identified. As a result, there is no evidence from RCTs to determine the effects of administering the hepatitis B vaccine during pregnancy on the prevention of HBV infection in infants. This lack of evidence means that no clinical recommendations can currently be made regarding this intervention. The authors emphasize the need for well-designed randomized clinical trials to investigate the impact of hepatitis B vaccination during pregnancy on the rate of infant infection and to evaluate any potential adverse effects associated with this approach.
